extracted.intended_audience: princes, courtiers, and readers seeking guidance on courtly conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts of Castiglione's normative guidance about the qualities, aims, and practical behaviour of the ideal courtier and his relation to a prince; describes what a courtier should be able to do and avoid. Useful for evaluating or prescribing courtly conduct in a Renaissance/early-modern courtly context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of the perfect Courtier (win prince's favour to speak truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: So to win for himself, by means of the accomplishments ascribed to him, the favour and mind of the prince whom he serves, that he may be able to say, and always shall say, the truth about everything which it is fitting for the prince to know, without fear or risk of giving offence thereby; and that when he sees his prince's mind inclined to do something wrong, he may be quick to oppose, and gently to make use of the favour acquired by his good accomplishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Courtier's chief end is instrumental: attain the prince's confidence through accomplishments so that one may candidly counsel and correct the prince. The capacity to speak truth and oppose wrongdoing is the measure of the Courtier's usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of accomplishments (skills and ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Being nobly born, graceful, agreeable, and expert in so many exercises (dancing, merry-making, singing and playing, music, festivals, games, arms, horses, verses, and the like).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These arts are the 'flower' of Courtiership — they are expected accomplishments. However, they are valuable only insofar as they serve the higher end of guiding the prince; otherwise they risk becoming frivolous vanities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readiness of wit, pleasantness, shrewdness, and knowledge of letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessing the goodness described together with readiness of wit and pleasantness, and shrewdness and knowledge of letters and many other things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social intelligence, liveliness, and literary/cultural knowledge are instruments used to charm the prince and to make moral and political counsel effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pleasure as a means to inculcate virtue (moral craftiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Courtier put the veil of pleasure to such a use ... now with music, now with arms and horses, now with verses, now with love talk ... like cunning doctors, who often anoint the edge of the cup with a sweet cordial, when they wish to give some bitter-tasting medicine to sick and over-delicate children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix agreeable entertainments with moral instruction so the prince accepts and internalizes virtuous precepts; pleasant accomplishments should be used tactically to make difficult counsel palatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and opposition to falsehood and flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: That man's mind tends to the best end who purposes to see to it that his prince shall be deceived by no one, shall hearken not to flatterers or to slanderers and liars, and shall distinguish good and evil, and love the one and hate the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Courtier must be a bulwark against falsehood: avoid flattery, speak truth, and expose deceivers. Falsehood (flattery) is named as the root of ignorance and self-esteem that corrupt princes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of a truly good end and ability to find fitting means
rubrics_metrics.description: The merit of well-doing lies chiefly in two things, one of which is the choice of an end for our intentions that shall be truly good, and the other ability to find means suitable and fitting to conduce to that good end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of the Courtier depends on both his aims (must be morally good, e.g., the betterment of the prince/state) and his practical skill in selecting appropriate means (accomplishments, persuasion) to reach that end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical use of accomplishments; prohibition of corrupt courtiers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no punishment so harsh and cruel as to be a sufficient penalty for those wicked courtiers who use their gentle and pleasant ways and fine accomplishments to a bad end, and therewith seek their prince's favour, in order to corrupt him and entice him from the path of virtue and lead him into vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An anti-pattern: using courtly arts to obtain power for corrupting the prince is morally condemnable; the Courtier must not pursue self-interest at the expense of the prince's virtue or the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation of moral virtues through instruction and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In virtue it is necessary to have a master, who by instruction and good reminders shall arouse and awake in us those moral virtues ... and like a good husbandman shall cultivate them ... custom creates in us the habit of both the one and the other, so that we first practise virtue or vice, and then are virtuous or vicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtues (justice, shame, continence, etc.) are not purely natural gifts but can and should be taught and habituated. Good manners (eating, drinking, speaking, walking, gestures) are part of this cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession and cultivation of justice and shame (modesty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice and shame, which you say Jove sent upon earth to all men, are natural in each one of us. But ... nature alone is not enough, there is need of studied practice and of reason, to purify and clear the soul ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These core moral dispositions must be developed by study and practice; laws and social training presuppose that people can learn such virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding effeminacy, vanities, and purely ornamental devices
rubrics_metrics.description: These elegances, devices, mottoes, and other like things that pertain to discourse about women and love ... often serve only to effeminate the mind, to corrupt youth, and to reduce it to great wantonness of living; whence ... but few are to be found who dare ... to run into danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accomplishments and ornament must be tempered; avoid letting display, mottos, and love-games degenerate into weakness and avoidance of noble actions (e.g., courage in war and public duty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical exempla and public honours to incite virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: He will be able to incite his prince by the example of the famous captains and other eminent men ... and to erect the same in public places, both for the honor of these men and as a stimulus to others, so that they might be led by worthy emulation to strive to reach that glory too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing admired precedents (statues, public honors) and encouraging emulation of great exemplars is an effective means for a Courtier to promote virtuous conduct in the prince and populace.
